pages.title: What is Not a “Collection”?
bullets: Most of our variables have one value in them - when we put a new value in the variable, the old value is overwritten

$ python
>>> x = 2
>>> x = 4
>>> print(x)
4
pages.pdf_text:
What is Not a “Collection”?
Most of our variables have one value in them - when we put a new
value in the variable, the old value is overwritten
$ python
>>> x = 2
>>> x = 4
>>> print(x)
4

pages.title: A List is a Kind of Collection
bullets:
A collection allows us to put many values in a single “variable”
A collection is nice because we can carry all many values around in one convenient package.

friends = [ 'Joseph', 'Glenn', 'Sally' ]

carryon = [ 'socks', 'shirt', 'perfume' ]
pages.pdf_text:

pages.title: List Constants
bullets:
List constants are surrounded by square brackets and the elements in the list are separated by commas
A list element can be any Python object - even another list
A list can be empty
pages.pdf_text:
List Constants
• List constants are surrounded by
square brackets and the elements
in the list are separated by
commas
• A list element can be any Python
object - even another list
• A list can be empty
>>> print([1, 24, 76])
[1, 24, 76]
>>> print(['red', 'yellow',
'blue'])
['red', 'yellow', 'blue']
>>> print(['red', 24, 98.6])
['red', 24, 98.6]
>>> print([ 1, [5, 6], 7])
[1, [5, 6], 7]
>>> print([])
[]

pages.title: Lists are Mutable
bullets:
Strings are “immutable” - we cannot change the contents of a string - we must make a new string to make any change
Lists are “mutable” - we can change an element of a list using the index operator

>>> fruit = 'Banana'
>>> fruit[0] = 'b'
Traceback 
TypeError: 'str' object does not 
support item assignment
>>> x = fruit.lower()
>>> print(x)
banana
>>> lotto = [2, 14, 26, 41, 63]
>>> print(lotto)
[2, 14, 26, 41, 63]
>>> lotto[2] = 28
>>> print(lotto)
[2, 14, 28, 41, 63]

pages.title: How Long is a List?
bullets:
The len() function takes a list as a parameter and returns the number of elements in the list
Actually len() tells us the number of elements of any set or sequence (such as a string...)

>>> greet = 'Hello Bob'
>>> print(len(greet))
9
>>> x = [ 1, 2, 'joe', 99]
>>> print(len(x))
4
>>>

pages.title: Using the range Function
bullets:
The range function returns a list of numbers that range from zero to one less than the parameter
We can construct an index loop using for and an integer iterator

>>> print(range(4))
[0, 1, 2, 3]
>>> friends = ['Joseph', 'Glenn', 'Sally']
>>> print(len(friends))
3
>>> print(list(range(len(friends))))
[0, 1, 2]
>>>
pages.pdf_text:

pages.title: A Tale of Two Loops...
bullets:
Happy New Year: Joseph
Happy New Year: Glenn
Happy New Year: Sally

>>> print(len(friends))
3
>>> print(list(range(len(friends))))

>>>
pages.pdf_text:
A Tale of Two Loops...
friends = ['Joseph', 'Glenn', 'Sally']
for friend in friends :
    print('Happy New Year:',  friend)
for i in range(len(friends)) :
    friend = friends[i]
    print('Happy New Year:',  friend)
Happy New Year: Joseph
Happy New Year: Glenn
Happy New Year: Sally
>>> friends = ['Joseph', 'Glenn', 'Sally']
>>> print(len(friends))
3
>>> print(list(range(len(friends))))
[0, 1, 2]
>>>

pages.title: Concatenating Lists Using +
bullets: We can create a new list by adding two existing lists together
pages.pdf_text:
Concatenating Lists Using +
We can create a new list
by adding two existing
lists together
>>> a = [1, 2, 3]
>>> b = [4, 5, 6]
>>> c = a + b
>>> print(c)
[1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6]
>>> print(a)
[1, 2, 3]

pages.title: Lists Can Be Sliced Using :
bullets: Remember:  Just like in strings, the second number is “up to but not including”
pages.pdf_text:
Lists Can Be Sliced Using :
>>> t = [9, 41, 12, 3, 74, 15]
>>> t[1:3]
[41,12]
>>> t[:4]
[9, 41, 12, 3]
>>> t[3:]
[3, 74, 15]
>>> t[:]
[9, 41, 12, 3, 74, 15]
Remember:  Just like in
strings, the second
number is “up to but not
including”

pages.title: Building a List from Scratch
bullets:
We can create an empty list and then add elements using the append method
The list stays in order and new elements are added at the end of the list

>>> stuff = list()
>>> stuff.append('book')
>>> stuff.append(99)
>>> print(stuff)
['book', 99]
>>> stuff.append('cookie')
>>> print(stuff)
['book', 99, 'cookie']
pages.pdf_text:

pages.title: Is Something in a List?
bullets:
Python provides two operators that let you check if an item is in a list
These are logical operators that return True or False
They do not modify the list

>>> some = [1, 9, 21, 10, 16]
>>> 9 in some
True
>>> 15 in some
False
>>> 20 not in some
True
>>>

pages.title: Lists are in Order
bullets:
A list can hold many items and keeps those items in the order until we do something to change the order
A list can be sorted (i.e., change its order)
The sort method (unlike in strings) means “sort yourself”

>>> friends = [ 'Joseph', 'Glenn', 'Sally' ]
>>> friends.sort()
>>> print(friends)
['Glenn', 'Joseph', 'Sally']
>>> print(friends[1])
Joseph
>>>

pages.title: Built-in Functions and Lists
bullets:
There are a number of functions built into Python that take lists as parameters
Remember the loops we built?  These are much simpler.

>>> nums = [3, 41, 12, 9, 74, 15]
>>> print(len(nums))
6
>>> print(max(nums))
74
>>> print(min(nums))
3
>>> print(sum(nums))
154
>>> print(sum(nums)/len(nums))
25.6

pages.title: Best Friends: Strings and Lists
bullets:
>>> abc = 'With three words'
>>> stuff = abc.split()
>>> print(stuff)
['With', 'three', 'words']
>>> print(len(stuff))
3
>>> print(stuff[0])
With

>>> print(stuff)
['With', 'three', 'words']
>>> for w in stuff :
...     print(w)
...
With
Three
Words
>>>
Split breaks a string into parts and produces a list of strings.  We think of these as words.  We can access a particular word or loop through all the words.
pages.pdf_text:

Split breaks a string into parts and produces a list of strings.  We think of these
as words.  We can access a particular word or loop through all the words.

bullets:
>>> line = 'A lot               of spaces'
>>> etc = line.split()
>>> print(etc)
['A', 'lot', 'of', 'spaces']
>>>
>>> line = 'first;second;third'
>>> thing = line.split()
>>> print(thing)
['first;second;third']
>>> print(len(thing))
1
>>> thing = line.split(';')
>>> print(thing)
['first', 'second', 'third']
>>> print(len(thing))
3
>>>

When you do not specify a delimiter, multiple spaces are treated like one delimiter

You can specify what delimiter character to use in the splitting
